after.title: The row and column Specht conventions in rank three
after.statement: Let $H=H_{A,q}(S_3)$, $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, and put $p_3(q)=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$. All four modules $P((3)),P((1^3)),C_{\mathrm M}((3)),C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ have rank1. On $P((3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((3))$, both generators act by $q$; on $P((1^3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$, both act by $-1$. In the canonical generators $x_{(3)},y_{(3)},c_{(3)},c_{(1^3)}$, the respective self-form values are $1,q^{-3}p_3(q),p_3(q),1$. Thus $\Phi_{(3)}(x_{(3)})=c_{(1^3)}$ has exact form multiplier $u_{(3)}=1$, whereas $\Phi_{(1^3)}(y_{(3)})=c_{(3)}$ has $u_{(1^3)}=q^3$. In both targets the action is twisted by $\theta$, so the two module identities match. At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the respective form values are $1,6,6,1$, and $\theta$ exchanges trivial and sign. These identities specialize over every commutative ring with a unit parameter. No choice principle is used.
after.strategy: For shape $(3)$ the row permutation module has one basis vector $x_{(3)}=\sum_wT_w$ with chosen norm1, and its ordinary polytabloid generator is $x_{(3)}$; pair the six Hecke terms to get $x_{(3)}T_i=qx_{(3)}$ and $x_{(3)}^2=p_3(q)x_{(3)}$. The latter identity gives the Murphy cell norm $p_3(q)$. For shape $(1^3)$ the row module is the regular module, and $y_{(3)}=\sum_w(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$ obeys $y_{(3)}T_i=-y_{(3)}$ by the same paired-term quadratic calculation. Its norm in the standard row basis is $\sum_wq^{-\ell(w)}=q^{-3}p_3(q)$, since the longest permutation has length3 and maps lengths to $3-\ell(w)$. The bottom Murphy quotient has generator1; modulo higher Murphy shapes, $1+T_i=0$, so $T_i=-1$ and its form has value1. The rank1 maps send the displayed generators as stated, and $\theta(T_i)=q-1-T_i$ exchanges the two actions. Direct comparison of norms proves both units. Evaluating $q=1$ gives the four stated integers; all identities were proved over the Laurent ring, so base change is legitimate even when $p_3(q)$ vanishes. No generic argument or quantum-factorial division is used.

after.title: The two-tableau pairing at a singular parameter
after.statement:
For $\lambda=(2,1)$ put $x=1+T_1$ and $b_0=x$, $b_1=xT_2$, $b_2=xT_2T_1$ in the row permutation module. Its form is $\operatorname{diag}(1,q,q^2)$ and its generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are $R_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&q&q-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $R_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1&0\\q&q-1&0\\0&0&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The ordinary polytabloid basis is $p_0=z=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$, $p_1=zT_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$. Their embedding has unit determinant on its $b_0,b_2$ coordinates, and their form is
$$B=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{pmatrix}.$$
In the Murphy quotient let $c_0=x$, $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher shape $(3)$. Its form and generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are
$$G=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_1=\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\q&q-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
On the ordinary basis the matrices are $P_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\-q^2&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $P_2=M_2$. The map $\Phi(p_0)=c_0$, $\Phi(p_1)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ has matrix $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; it satisfies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$. The same-shape perfect cross-pairing on the bases $(c_0,c_1)$ and $(p_0,p_1)$ has matrix $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $-q^2$, a unit; its entries are the row-form coefficients before quotienting. Thus the exact self-form multiplier is1. Both Gram determinants equal $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ over characteristic zero these forms are nonsingular with determinant $-1$, even though $[2]_q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic2 both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and have radical0. This distinguishes a singular algebra parameter from degeneracy of this particular module form. No choice principle is used.
after.strategy: The row module action follows by the Hecke quadratic and braid relations: $b_0T_1=qb_0$, $b_1T_1=b_2$, $b_2T_1=qb_1+(q-1)b_2$; $b_0T_2=b_1$, $b_1T_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1$, $b_2T_2=qb_2$. Substituting the displayed $p_0,p_1$ gives $p_0T_1=-p_0$, $p_1T_1=-q^2p_0+qp_1$, $p_0T_2=p_1$, $p_1T_2=qp_0+(q-1)p_1$. The projection of $p_0,p_1$ onto coordinates $b_0,b_2$ has matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-q^{-1}\\q&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant1, proving a split free rank2 submodule over every ring. It contains the generator and is stable under both Hecke generators, so it is exactly $zH$, without using a general polytabloid-basis theorem. In the Murphy cell quotient the higher vector $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ vanishes, so $b_2=-c_0-c_1$; the preceding action gives $M_i$. Cell multiplication gives $G_{00}=q+1$, $G_{01}=-1$, $G_{11}=q(q+1)-(q-1)=q^2+1$. Computing the row-basis weighted inner products gives $B$. Direct matrix multiplication verifies both intertwining identities and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$; $\det A=-1$ is a unit. Evaluating the two Gram matrices gives the stated radicals. Exact integer-polynomial verification is recorded separately in rank-three-symbolic-check.json; that finite check supports these calculations and is not a proof of the general comparison theorem.

before.title: Untwisted conjugation changes the module
before.statement: Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$, the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1,1,1))$ is the sign module with $T_i=-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its dual are the trivial module with $T_i=1$. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ}$ without the twist $\theta$ is false in general; the correct statement is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with $\theta$ the sign automorphism. This reproduces the actual source-20 root countermodel using only the new foundations of this pair. No choice principle is used.

after.title: Untwisted conjugation changes the module
after.statement: Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$, the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ is sign with $T_i=-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its contragredient dual are trivial with $T_i=1$. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ without $\theta$ is false in general. The correct bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$; combining it with same-shape duality gives $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$, which is a different formula. This reproduces the source20 countermodel from the standalone new foundations. No choice principle is used.
after.strategy: The top row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ spans $P((3))$ and is fixed by every permutation, so this module and its dual are trivial. In the one-dimensional bottom Murphy cell, the higher elements $1+s_1$ and $1+s_2$ vanish, so each $s_i=-1$. A module isomorphism from the bottom cell to the trivial module would intertwine these scalar operators; over $\mathbb Q$, $-1\ne1$, so no such nonzero isomorphism exists. The automorphism $\theta$ sends $s_i$ to $-s_i$ and therefore corrects the action. The general corrected formulas follow by the two separately proved bridge theorems, not by treating the ordinary Specht module as always self-dual. This finite counterexample uses no Schur theory or old convention definition.

before.title: Polytabloid specialization and the exact signed multiplicity dictionary
before.statement: Assume the isomorphism and unit identity of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]. For every field $F$ at $q=1$, $P(\lambda)$ specializes to the ordinary integral-polytabloid Specht module $F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ of [[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], with its standard form, and $\theta$ becomes tensoring with the sign representation; this specialization is compatible with [[lem-conjugate-specht-sign-duality-over-fields]]. For an arbitrary unit $q$ over a field, $[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$ whenever $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$, and the simultaneous $q$-twist is the same $\theta$ on both sides. For a Schur corner already proved to send the Weyl module $W(\lambda)$ to $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and its head $L(\lambda)$ to $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$, the ordinary dictionary is $F(W(\lambda'))\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $F(L(\lambda'))\cong(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta$, including zero; it is never the untwisted conjugate-dual identity. No Schur-algebra or source-20 convention result is a prerequisite of this conditional dictionary. No choice principle is used.
before.strategy: Conditional corollary: its proof composes the escalated theorem [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] with published q=1 facts, so it is escalated as a consumer. The q=1 specialization clause, once the theorem is available: at $q=1$ the Hecke algebra is $\mathbb C[S_n]$ ([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]), the elements $x_\lambda,y_{\lambda'}$ become the row sum and the column antisymmetrizer, so $z_\lambda$ becomes the integral polytabloid generator and $P(\lambda)_{q=1}$ is the ordinary integral-polytabloid Specht lattice of [[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]]; $\theta$ at $q=1$ acts as $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$, so the theorem reads $S^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong(S^{\lambda'})^*$, which is the published [[lem-conjugate-specht-sign-duality-over-fields]]; unwinding the comparison in the other order gives the dictionary. The multiplicity clause is formal from exactness and simplicity preservation of $(-)^\theta$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]])(2). The Schur-corner clause is a conditional application only: it quantifies over corners already proved to carry the stated functoriality and is not a backward dependency on any Schur-algebra or source-20 result. The precise state of the gap is recorded in the batch notes; no invented unit and no unconditional Schur identity is asserted. No choice principle is used.

after.strategy: At $q=1$, the row basis $x_\lambda w$ maps to the ordinary row tabloid of $t^\lambda\cdot w$. This is a bijection of the distinguished bases and preserves the form because all diagonal weights become1. The vector $x_\lambda w_\lambda y_{\lambda'}$ maps exactly to the column antisymmetrizer applied to the column-filled tabloid of shape $\lambda$: the rows of $t^{\lambda'}$ are precisely its consecutive column label blocks. Hence its group-algebra orbit is the ordinary integral-polytabloid Specht lattice; the proved split inclusion and integral basis commute with every field base change, so this is an actual module-and-form identification over every field, not an extension of a complex-only theorem. In particular $\theta(w)=\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$. The signed conjugate bridge and its unit form factor identify $P(\lambda)$ with $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ and $D_{\mathrm{DJ}}^\mu$ with $(D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu'})^\theta$, including zero quotients. Applying the same exact involutive pullback to a finite composition series proves the multiplicity equality; no form must be nonsingular. Finally the conditional Schur premises give $F(W(\lambda'))=C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $F(L(\lambda'))=D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda'}\cong(D_{\mathrm{DJ}}^\lambda)^\theta$.
